data.name: Jamna
data.gender_notes: Jamna is used as a unisex name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Jamna is a Sanskrit name derived from the goddess of prosperity and wealth, Yama. She is known for bringing abundance and good fortune. In Hindu mythology, Yama is the god of death and the ruler of the underworld, but his wife, Yamuna, embodies the nurturing and prosperous aspects of the deity. The name Jamna carries the meaning “Goddess of prosperity” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Jamna usually hope their child will grow to embody goddess of prosperity and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.etymology: Jamna belongs to the Sanskrit linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Goddess of prosperity.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Jamna total 3, giving a life-path number of 3. Number 3 is linked with Jupiter and with the qualities of creativity, expression and optimism.

historical_references.reference: Jamna is identified with the river Goddess Ganga in some Hindu texts and mythology. The name Jamna is mentioned in the ancient Indian epic Mahabharata, which describes a famous battle between the Pandava brothers and their cousins, the Kauravas. During this war, Arjuna, one of the Pandava brothers, was given the divine chariot 'Apsara-sena' by the celestial nymph Menaka. This chariot had the river Goddess Ganga as its banner or flag. Arjuna called out to the Goddess, addressing her as 'Jamnavati', meaning 'dwelling of Jamna'. This suggests that Jamna may have been a prominent deity or river goddess in ancient India.

historical_references.reference: Another reference to Jamna can be found in the Hindu Puranas, where she is described as the wife of the sage Rishi Agastya. Agastya is believed to have performed severe penance to please Lord Shiva, and as a result, he was granted a boon that his wife Jamna would never desert him. This suggests that Jamna may have been an important figure in Hinduism, particularly in relation to the cult of sages and their wives.
